body: January sun comes in low across the quad at twenty past seven and lands on Theo’s half of 412: the made bed, the shoes in their line under it, the orange hat hung on the bedpost by its brim. Theo stands in the middle of it at the mirror on the inside of the closet door, knotting a tie for the Sigma Rho rush breakfast. The navy blazer is already on and buttoned. He wears it like a dare.
On the dresser his iPhone buzzes, quits, and buzzes again. Theo finishes the knot, looks at it, takes it apart and starts over.
“Brooks,” he says. “Brooks Callahan would like me to know that eggs are at eight. He has told me three times since six. That’s leadership.”

Jack is on the edge of his own bed with one shoe on. Theo picks the phone up off the dresser, wakes it, and turns to face the room, and this morning he reads Jack the News Feed in the voice: the lector at the twelve-ten doing the intentions, slow, a little through the nose, every name given its full weight.

body: He turns the phone around and holds it out across the gap between the beds, so Jack can see it at the size it is: a candle stuck upright in a dinner roll, and behind it Lena in the gray cardigan, smiling at whoever held the camera, and Julian’s arm along the back of her chair.

“For Julian Park-Ellis,” Theo reads, “who had a birthday.” He touches the likes open and reads them down, without inflection. “Tess Broussard Fontenot. Laney Price. Remy Broussard. Kenzie Rourke. Peter Haddad.” And nine more Jack has never heard of, each in the same voice, to the end of the list. “Lord, hear our prayer.”
Jack has the shoelace in both hands.
Monday night she said *call me after*, and he didn’t.

Theo turns the phone back to himself. “For the rush committee of Sigma Rho,” he reads off nothing at all, “which meets over eggs at eight to decide my worth.” A pause, for the congregation. “Lord, hear our prayer.”

The phone goes into the inside pocket of the blazer. He goes back to the mirror and tightens a knot that doesn’t need it, and in the glass his eyes find Jack’s and go back to the knot. He has been like this since Sunday night: courteous, exact, a host with a houseguest he happens to like. No *Father Jack*. No second congratulations. Not a word about the girl with the three hundred and ninety-one.
“Rush,” Theo says, “is a job interview where they also throw you in a pool.”
“You want it?” Jack says.

Theo looks at the knot in the glass. “Yes,” he says. And, at more length: “They have a house on the bluff, a chef named Hector who does omelets to order on Sundays, and a composite photograph in the front hall going back to 1971 in which no one has ever smiled. I’d be the first.”
“Are they throwing you in a pool?”

“Costigan. It’s January. They’re throwing me in the *ocean*. Brooks has a wetsuit for the ones they like.” He turns the collar of the blazer up, looks at it, turns it down. At the door, at twenty-eight past: “Eggs and judgment.”
When he’s gone, Jack says it for him, under his breath. “Lord, hear our prayer.”
The RAZR goes on the desk at 7:31. It’s half past ten at Ursuline, between periods.

body: Ma’s can has been on his desk since Saturday night, beside the lamp, where it’s the first thing he sees: the Café du Monde can, empty, washed, the lid pressed back on. He picks it up. He stands on the desk chair with it, the chair swiveling a little under him, to put it on the top shelf of the closet, where he won’t see it every morning.

The shelf runs the width of the closet, split down the middle by a plywood divider somebody put in before either of them was born. His half is bare. He sets the can on it, and from up on the chair he can see over the divider onto Theo’s: the gray camera bag; the shoebox, COOKIES — DON’T; the crook of the Burberry hooked over the front edge. At the back, where the black duffel sat all fall, the dust has kept its shape, a clean rectangle with the corners worn round. There is nothing else.

In September, at ten past one in the morning, a jean jacket came up out of a black bag into his hands, Our Lady on the back. On the morning of the first storm in December, a red Ferris wheel on a collar, two inches of it, where a zipper had come open. The week before Christmas, at two in the morning on the wall at the Point, Lena, with a letter she had by heart: *They never found it.* This morning: a gray camera bag, a shoebox, an umbrella, and a clean place in the dust.

journal.title: The shelf
journal.text: The black bag isn’t on the top shelf in 412 anymore.

The garment bag on the back of the door holds a tuxedo and a dry cleaner’s plastic and nothing else. The bottom of the closet is boots and a tennis racket in a wooden press. Not in 412.
He puts every shoe back with the toes squared to the bed frame, the way Theo squares them, and stands the racket where it was. The closet door won’t latch unless you lift it. He lifts it.

He gets down off the chair. The closet door won’t latch unless you lift it, so he lifts it.

The closet door won’t latch unless you lift it. He lifts it, and hears it catch.

s02.slug: TUESDAY · 9:10 AM · DELGADO HALL, THE MAILBOXES
body: The mailboxes on two are a wall of little brass doors, each with a window the size of a stamp and a combination nobody remembers past October, and the radiator under them knocks twice and thinks about a third. Down the hall somebody shuffles toward the showers in slippers, and a hair dryer starts up behind a door and stops. Jack is down from four with his bag on his shoulder and twenty minutes before a nine-thirty, and Lena and Laney are ahead of him at the wall.

Laney has her sunglasses on indoors and the Pi Lam hood up. Lena is in the navy peacoat buttoned to the top, her hair up off her neck with a pencil through it, and she has a yellow package slip from the front desk in both hands and is reading it.
Laney sees him first. She turns to her mailbox and opens it, and takes out nothing, and studies that through the sunglasses.

body.text: His *tomorrow*, sent from 412 on Sunday night, never got an answer. Lena reads the slip to the bottom, the fine print too, before she looks up.
body.else: Lena reads the slip to the bottom, the fine print too, before she looks up.

body: “Morning, Jack.”
“Morning.”
She folds the slip in half, and in half again. “How was the rest of your break?”

She heard most of it on the phone already, every night of it, from the garage. She lets him tell it again like news. He starts with Saturday: Nonna going through the housedress for the twenty, left pocket, right pocket, left again, a butterscotch, a holy card, *per il viaggio*. Rosie’s drawing of the plane, with the crab belted into the next seat, on the aisle, in case. Pop at the Departures curb, *thirty seconds*, and still there with the hazards going when Jack looked back through the glass, explaining something to a man in a vest.
“How’s her hand?” Lena says. It’s the question you ask.
“Better. She found the twenty with it.”
“Good.”

He tells the rest well. He knows where the laughs are in it; he has told her worse things better, at two in the morning, and had her laughing till she had to put the phone down. She listens with the slip folded small in her fingers and her eyes on his collar.
“And Ma says to tell you it was good coffee.” He hears how it sounds and adds the rest. “She said to use those words.”
Lena looks at him properly, the first time this morning. “Tell her I’m glad.”
Laney shuts her mailbox on nothing.
Then Denver, and a man from Grand Junction who fell asleep on his shoulder somewhere over Kansas and woke up apologizing and kept apologizing until Colorado —
And he stops. He got as far as Denver.
She doesn’t ask for the rest. “That sounds lovely, Jack.”

choices.text: “You said you had a baptism’s worth to tell me.”
choices.key: At the mailboxes Lena asked about your break, and you told her as far as Denver. When you asked for her baptism’s worth, she said it was lovely.
response: “You said you had a baptism’s worth to tell me.”
Lena puts the slip in her bag. “She wore the gown,” she says. “It was lovely.”
On the kitchen phone in Youngstown the gown had a cedar chest in Breaux Bridge, and a storm it rode out in it. This morning it got one word.
Laney takes her arm.
“Have a lovely —” Lena says, and hears it, and stops on it. “Have a good day, Jack.”

They go down the hall toward the stairs with the slip and the sunglasses. Jack opens his own box. Behind the little window there’s a half-sheet folded once, NEWMAN — SPRING RETREAT, and under it a mountain somebody drew with a ruler.

s06.slug: TUESDAY · 8:00 PM · ST. BRENDAN THE NAVIGATOR — THE CHURCH, THEN THE NEWMAN HALL
body: St. Brendan’s is full on a Tuesday night the way it’s full on Ash Wednesday. Every pew under the hull of the ceiling, and students down the side aisle sitting on the floor with their backpacks between their knees, and townspeople Jack has never seen at a twelve-ten, a woman in hospital scrubs with her car keys still in her hand. At the Marian shrine the votive rack is lit nearly to the last row, and the heat of it comes off the brass, and somebody has propped a sheet of printer paper against the rail with one word on it in marker, HAITI, and nothing under it, because there is nothing yet to write. A boy Jack knows from the Commons line kneels on the bare floor in a Lakers jersey. Two girls from the Thursday Bible study are holding hands in the side aisle. Up in the loft Gus Ferreira has the organ down so low it’s more floor than sound.

Fr. Osei comes out in his black clerical shirt and doesn’t go to the ambo. He stands at the foot of the sanctuary step with his hands folded. “We know very little tonight,” he says, “and I will not pretend we know more; we know that they are our brothers and sisters, and that the Mother of God does not need the telephone lines to be working.”
He steps aside, and from the second pew Lena leads the decade.
“The first Sorrowful Mystery. The Agony in the Garden.”

Her voice reaches the back without being raised. Two weeks ago it was in his ear every night, from her back steps, from behind her father’s register, from the river. Now it’s coming from the second pew, and he’s six pews back, and it’s for everybody. *Our Father*, and the church comes in under her, the old men a beat early and the students a beat late, and then the first Hail Mary.

Julian is beside her, sitting back while the whole pew kneels, his hands loose between his knees. He doesn’t pretend. He has the second half by heart now, and when the church answers he answers too, low, a word behind everyone, careful with it.

Jack starts the first Hail Mary on his own count, quick, the Glenwood Avenue speed, Nonna’s, the words worn flat as a step. By the second Hail Mary he is on hers. Somewhere in the sixth he stops hearing it as her voice and hears it as the count. *Now, and at the hour.* A full church says it ten times, slower than he has ever said it, and on half an island under Cuba there are people under concrete in the dark, and Gus keeps the organ under all of them, a tune half the room could hum.
After the Glory Be, Osei blesses them, and Gus brings the organ up for the first time and takes the hymn through once from the top, and the church sits and listens to it with its coats on.
At half past eight the Newman hall is folding chairs, the urn, a smell of burnt coffee and radiator, forty people in their coats, and Lena with a clipboard.

She has had it since before the decade. Clipped to it: the Catholic Relief Services page, printed in the office and still warm at one corner; a table schedule for tomorrow on the Commons Lawn, ten to five, two-hour shifts; a one-page cash-box protocol, numbered; the diocese’s number for the deposit, written in her hand along the top margin. She has a pencil through her hair and a second one behind her ear for when somebody walks off with the first. Peter Haddad, the Newman president, starts to say something about forming a committee, and inside two minutes he is holding the end of the tape while she puts up the sign-up sheet, and asking her where she wants the chairs. Becca is at the urn with Kevin, setting out cups in rows of ten. Jack is by the wall with a roll of masking tape somebody handed him, and when Lena needs the wall she reaches past him for it. “Excuse me, Jack.” Her sleeve goes by his. She smells of the votive rack.

Julian comes in from the parking lot with two cartons of the parish’s empty coffee cans for collection jars and sets them by the urn, and when the urn’s spigot sticks he jiggles the switch twice without being shown, which is what it takes, and goes back out for the next load.
She gives the orders in a whisper.

She doesn’t raise her voice once. The hall is loud, forty people and the urn coming to a boil, and every time she has the next thing to say she says it lower, barely over her breath, and forty people lean in to hear it.

Jack has watched her argue for five months, at tables and on roofs and down a phone line at one in the morning. He has never watched her do this. “Money. Not cans, not clothes. Cans sit in a warehouse in Miami. They need money.” Money to CRS, every dollar, by check or cash, and receipts written by hand. Two to a shift. The box never leaves the table and is never alone with one person. “Nobody makes change out of the box. If somebody needs change, they give the smaller bill.”

“Who has a car at nine tomorrow?” Peter does. “Then you take the box out to the Commons at nine and the bank bag back at five, and Mrs. Fitch has the key, and nobody else does.” Somebody who can letter is wanted for the sign; Kenzie can letter. Somebody with a folding table that isn’t the one with the broken leg; the one with the broken leg is Newman’s, and it goes in the closet with a note on it in Lena’s hand.
Kenzie Rourke, the cantor, puts her hand halfway up. “Can we go? Like — down there? My cousin did a mission trip to Honduras —”
“Not this week,” Lena says. “This week they need surgeons and money. We’re the money.”

Tyler Brandt has been waiting by the piano. “Brother,” he says to Peter, and then corrects course to Lena. “Before anything else — shouldn’t we have a holy hour? Exposition. All night, if we have to.”
“We just prayed,” Lena says. “Thursday, nine to midnight, the chapel’s yours. Put it on the sheet and ask Father.” Tyler writes it on the sheet, in capitals, and underlines it, and looks very happy.
Mrs. Fitch has a checkbook open on her knee. “I’ll bring lemon bars. A dollar.” She writes the check. “They’re worth two.”
“Lemon bars, Mrs. Fitch.” Lena writes it down.
A sophomore by the window wants to do a 5K. Somebody else wants a Facebook group. “Yes,” Lena says, to both, “after. Tomorrow is the table,” and they write their names down for the table instead.
Near the front a girl with a violin case between her feet puts her hand straight up, as if she’s in school. “I could play. At the table. People stop for a violin.”
“Name?”
“Clare. Dominguez.”
“Two to three, Clare. Thank you.”
Over at the urn Kevin is filling the reservoir out of a gallon jug, very carefully, for the whole time the girl is talking, and he goes on pouring a little after it’s full.

In the doorway of the office, at the side of the hall, Fr. Osei has the phone to his ear, his reading glasses off and swinging on their cord, and he puts the receiver down and picks it up and dials again, and listens, and puts it down.

Peter, beside Jack at the sign-up sheet, says it low. “He’s been calling a doctor in Port-au-Prince since five. A friend from medical school, from Ghana. Yaw. He works at a hospital down there.” He tears off a strip of tape with his teeth. “Nothing goes through.”
Osei comes to the doorway when the room is busy and looks at them all, the forty and the urn and the lemon bars, and somebody near him asks him how he is.
“I asked the bishop if he could spare an old doctor,” Osei says. “He said he couldn’t spare a young priest.”
Mrs. Fitch laughs first, at exactly the size it needs, and the room follows her a little way, and Osei goes back in to the phone.
Lena works down the sheet name by name, a tick for each. She reaches his.
“Jack. Wednesday, one to three. With Becca.”
At the urn Becca turns around with a stack of cups and waves the stack at him.
Lena’s pen waits on the next line. She is looking at the sheet. “We need hands. Who else can you bring?”

response: “Skye wants to help.”
It is the first time he has said it to her, out loud, in a room.
“Then bring her.”
She writes it on the sheet beside his name, *+1 (Jack)*, and the pen runs a stroke too long and leaves a tail on the 1.
“Kenzie,” she says. “Wednesday, three to five.”

“Then ask Sigma Rho.” The pen goes to the next line. “Kenzie. Wednesday, three to five.”

“Thank you.” The pen goes to the next line. “Kenzie. Wednesday, three to five.”

body: The Newman lounge has the couch with the spring that finds you, a crucifix over the bookshelf, and the television on its rolling cart, on CNN with the sound up. Ten of them are on the couch arms and the carpet folding the half-sheets for the table in thirds — CATHOLIC RELIEF SERVICES · HAITI EARTHQUAKE RESPONSE · EVERY DOLLAR — and stacking them in piles of fifty. Lena is on the end of the couch with her stack on the cushion beside her, running her thumbnail down every fold. Julian is on the floor at the other end with his own pile. Kevin is on the arm of a chair folding with hospital corners, which no one has asked him to do. Jack has the carpet by the coffee table and paper cuts on two fingers.

The room is quiet except for the paper. Earlier the anchor read out what the President said at the White House, that the country stands ready to help, and before that a woman from the Red Cross who said it was too soon to know, and said it three ways. Kenzie asks once if anyone minds the volume and no one answers her, and she leaves it. Lena hasn’t looked at the television since they started. She looks at the folds.

On the screen there are still photographs, one after another: a white wall come down across a street; a woman sitting on a curb with gray dust in her hair and on her arms; men with their bare hands in a heap of broken block. Over them, a reporter’s voice on a telephone line from Port-au-Prince, breaking up and coming back. He is standing outside a building that came down. There are people under it. You can hear them calling from the street, he says. He says nobody has equipment. He says they are *trapped*, and the line goes, and the anchor in Atlanta says his name twice.
Lena squares her stack on the cushion, edges even, and gets up and goes out of the room. She doesn’t make a sound doing it.
Julian is up before Jack has moved — a hand on the door frame, and he’s through it.
On the couch, where her stack was, the cushion hasn’t come back up yet.

choices.key: When the TV said trapped, Lena left the room and Julian went after her. You followed, and saw them on the back steps.
response: He puts his stack down and goes out the way they went, down the hall past the office, where Father is still dialing, to the door at the end of it.

choices.key: When the TV said trapped, Lena left the room and Julian went after her. You stayed and folded the flyers, and Julian came back and thanked you.
response: He stays on the carpet. Julian’s pile is on the floor where he left it, half done, the top sheet creased in the wrong place, and Jack pulls it over and refolds that one and goes on through the rest, his and Julian’s both, in thirds, piles of fifty.
Laney comes through from the hall with her coat over her arm, going the way Lena went. At the coffee table she stops long enough to look at him, sunglasses pushed up into her hair, and then she goes.
Ten minutes later Julian comes back by himself. He sits down on the carpet where he was and takes his half off the top of Jack’s pile, the folded half, and squares it.
“She’s okay,” he says. “She just needed air.” He looks at the stack. “Thanks.”

He folds beside Jack after that, on the carpet, not talking, and Jack doesn’t either. Julian’s folds come out straighter than his. On the television they have a map up now with a red circle on it, and then the President again, and then the map.
Jack folds. The paper cut on his thumb opens on every crease, and he keeps going till the piles are even.

s06b.slug: TUESDAY · 9:34 PM · ST. BRENDAN’S, THE BACK STEPS BY THE COURTYARD
body: The door at the end of the hall has a push bar and a square of glass with wire in it. Beyond it is the courtyard: the olive tree, the sprinkler head on its pipe that hasn’t worked since anybody can remember, the one bulb over the sacristy door, and the three back steps down to the flagstones.

Jack’s hand is on the bar. He leans on it, and the door gives, and the night comes in around the edge, January and the olive and somebody’s cigarette from the street. His mouth is already open on her name. He shuts it.

Lena is on the second step with her arms around her knees and her back to him. Julian is on the step below her, sitting sideways, with his shoulder against her shin. He isn’t talking. He is looking at the olive tree, and his mouth is shut.
After a while he takes his cardigan off, a dark green one with leather buttons, and reaches up behind him and puts it over her shoulders, and goes back to the olive tree.

Her hand comes off her knee and finds the edge of the cardigan and holds it closed at her throat. Out on the street a car goes by slow, looking for parking, and its lights go across the top of the wall and the olive and the step and are gone. Somewhere behind Jack in the building the urn clicks off.
The bar is cold under Jack’s hand. He stands there with the door open a foot and the January coming in over his shoes, not going out, not going back. He could cross the flagstones in four steps.

Julian sees him. Over her head, across the courtyard light, he finds Jack in the gap of the door and gives him a small nod, decent, with nothing in it Jack can find but *it’s all right*. Lena doesn’t turn around.
Jack lets the door come back on him slowly, all the way, so it won’t bang. He goes back down the hall, past the office and the phone, to the lounge, and sits down on the carpet, and folds flyers.

s14.slug: WEDNESDAY · 10:35 PM · DELGADO HALL, THE LOBBY — THE FRONT DESK

body.text: He comes in from the curb at twenty-five to eleven.
body.else: He comes in from the Grove at twenty-five to eleven with eucalyptus on his shoes.

body: The lobby is down to its night lights. On the front desk Marcus’s radio is turned low to KCBX, a man on a bad line from Port-au-Prince and then a woman in a studio saying his name, and behind the desk Lena and Priya have the gray cash box open between them, and Priya’s CASH LOG, laminated, with a wet-erase marker on a string. The door of the RA safe under the desk stands open.

“Per the Residential Life Handbook,” Priya says, without being asked, because he’s standing there, “cash in excess of five hundred dollars does not sleep in a student room, Costigan. It sleeps in my safe.” She taps the laminate. “I made a log.”
“That’s in the handbook?”
“It is now.”

Lena signs the log. Priya countersigns it, and caps the marker, and uncaps it, and they count it once more together, the stacks laid out on the desk blotter: the ones and the fives, the tens, the checks under a binder clip. Lena does the twenties last. There is purple marker down the side of her hand from the sign, and a day of giving orders under her breath has left her almost no voice at all. She counts the twenties in a whisper anyway, every one, and Priya’s lips move with her.
Lena finishes the count before she looks up. She turns her clipboard around on the desk and pushes a pen across to him with it. “You had the box from one to three. Initial your shift.”
He initials it under Becca’s *B.L.* She turns the clipboard back around.

“Four thousand eight hundred and seventeen dollars and forty cents.” She squares the twenties and puts the band around them. “It goes in the safe tonight and to the diocese office at nine. Your table did the most.”

She lays the banded twenties in the box, and takes out one envelope that is fatter than the rest, and puts it back in again, square. “Skye’s envelope was the biggest. Tell her thank you. From Newman.”
She says it straight. Her hands are already closing the lid.

journal.title: Lena Broussard
journal.text: New Orleans. Two seventeen. Classics. Hale paired us for the semester. Makes a roux like she’s taking a vow and expects you to keep up. Her father sells Gulf shrimp — Broussard’s Seafood, Banks Street. Boyfriend: Wes Arceneaux — Tulane, civil engineering, the boat at sixteen. Calls at 8:04 on the dot. Her grandmother, Lucille Guidry, died in the storm in ’05; they buried her in November, in the good dress. The medal came back to her mother in a plastic bag. She has never asked her mother one question. The year after, she went to Mass every morning to yell at God, and somewhere in there it stopped being a fight. Paints a mean fleur-de-lis. Said hi to Danny. Says she’s going to be defense. Walked her home the long way from Pi Lam: the beach, the creek, the tower, the Commons, the Lagoon bench. Wes calls from somewhere loud lately; her brother Luc is with him. She’s decided not to notice. The Tuesday of the wake he called on the dot, from his room. He came for Columbus Day weekend to see the Pacific. She’d told him it’s a threat. He touched it at two in the morning. Came to Marisol for the money, she says — Notre Dame gave her half. Went to Hale’s office to tell him he was wrong about who gets to forgive. Cried for Anders on the roof and didn’t give an inch. Stayed till the chimes. There’s a sentence she hasn’t finished. Her middle name is Thérèse; October first is her feast. She erased *Show Lena* out of the Hopkins herself, so Danny could have it. At midnight I gave her *Story of a Soul* with my margins in it, and she wouldn’t let me erase a word. On the beach she asked if I know what I’m doing. I don’t. She laughed. At the elevator: ‘That was a terrible thing to be glad about.’ Brought Wes to everything. Wouldn’t walk past the last house on Seacliff toward the Point; said she was cold. At the stove she gave Becca the spoon. Monday night, two floors down, on the phone to New Orleans: ‘He’s my friend, Wes.’ Plays the piano in the Delgado basement — the one nobody admits to playing. Two years at the Rosary. At five in the morning she played the Saints on the Ferrer carillon with her fists, one bell flat, and said it wasn’t flat, it was New Orleans. Wes told her what I said on the beach, and what I didn’t. On a motel porch above Lucia at three in the morning she told me I can’t say her name like that. She asked what I decided. Not to be the one who wrecks anything, I said. She said okay. Then: me neither. Bought her Mémère a fruitcake from the monks, in exact change. ‘A girl writes the thing she wants first, Youngstown.’ Halloween: Flannery O’Connor, with a stuffed peacock tagged 57. Andalusia. She wouldn’t go past the last house on Seacliff, not even for Laney. ‘I came as her. I never said she was right.’ In the last minute of the extra hour, she put my hat back on. All Souls: she wrote her grandmother’s name in the book, and Nora Calloway’s. Nora was her host at Preview Weekend, in April. That night Wes ended it, on the phone, on the east stairs. He stopped going to Mass in September. There’s a ring. She knew something in September and decided not to notice — she says she’s good at it. At six in the morning she asked me what I’m going to do. She wrote Hale twelve pages in the spring of ’08, two years after the year she yelled at God. She’s had the same postcard the whole time. She knew mine on the porch. She had a house picked out on Zimple Street. A fig tree. She’d picked the paint. Veterans Day, on the bench above Campus Point: St. Martin gave the beggar half his cloak; she says everybody forgets the beggar took it. No. 9 for the reliquary. Friday the 13th, under the eucalyptus, in the middle of a sentence about monarchs: Julian asked her to dinner. So. Thursday night in the basement she played the piano properly — around the dead F. The last time she played it right in front of anybody was a November, four years ago. If you play well, she says, people ask you to play. Reading *New Moon* out of spite. Friday she signed the Manhattan Declaration from bed, with a cold. Two soups. She ate Julian’s. Mine’s on the sill for tomorrow. Ate Gloria’s soup cold out of the quart, at the sill, at six in the morning. Argued YES: a promise is made to a person, not to a reason. Wrote on my paper that I don’t believe one sentence of it. Neither does she. Mémère is lighting a candle for Nonna — the whole name. Half a name is half a candle. At the airport: Our Lady of Prompt Succor, for Nonna. She works fast. Thanksgiving: Theo said *pop* to the whole Broussard table. She asked about Theo, and Nonna, and her saint. Julian called during grace. Wes was in the kitchen. ‘Go back to your family, Youngstown.’ Handed Julian the bell rope at Sully’s. Knows I don’t work Mondays. Texted at two in the morning about Yusuf’s mother. On the lawn at four, looking at the place I wasn’t. Came to the Anchor at the end of my shift in Kevin’s car — Julian’s in Oakland, his brother’s home from the Navy. She has a paper. St. Nicholas Eve: Walgreens at half past one. I told her about Ma’s two hundred shoes; she said then we’re doing it, and we did every door in Delgado. Says I hold my phone like a hand of cards. Asked where I go. I said sometime. She said okay. Book Nine, for her Greek final: *Outis*. Nobody. In the laundry room she stepped back first. ‘Don’t make me be the one who wrecks something.’ Julian’s writing something she can’t hear yet. Twelve and oh in overtime. Her free hand found Kevin. Knows Book Nine by heart; asked me to pray at eight. Picked my best argument at the Brick: what a man says yes to. Put her phone face up next to mine and said nothing. Heard Julian’s song before anybody. ‘It’s good, Jack. It’s really good.’ Told me not to leave in the second chorus. The Advent party: I kept the whole room between us all night. She brought coffee to the white elephant, and I got it. Stole my 8-Ball. Won an argument about ‘Joy to the World’ with Isaac Watts. Didn’t play. Julian did. Friday night, half past twelve, she knocked on 412; Theo said the library. At the Mañanitas she told me about Juan Diego, who took the long way around the hill. Thirteen and oh. She texted me the number. After the Gaudete Mass she asked the 8-Ball something. Better not tell you now. Geminids from the roof without me. At Hale’s oral she’d answered him in Augustine — said my sentence was his. She defended it and won, and told him to ask where I say yes at two in the morning. Julian kissed her goodbye at his car; he’s going to New Orleans for New Year’s. Friday she knocked with two coffees and a list of every place. She played the basement piano for me, properly. Taught me a secret in the O Antiphons. Pecan at Gloria’s counter; fourteen and oh is ordained. On the Lighthouse porch she said it plain: I’d never not answered her before. Never missed Sully’s. Always came to her, whatever it was — and now I stay away. She knows something’s hurting. She didn’t make me say what. Walked past the last house to the Point for the first time all semester. The bonfires on the levee on Christmas Eve — call her from the garage. On the roof I nearly said it. The 8-Ball said ask again later. She gave me the tin to keep. I gave her Benedict. At the checkpoint she turned around and said something I couldn’t hear. Christmas week: her sister had the baby in the third quarter of the Dallas game, while they were still undefeated, so Beau didn’t get a vote. Lucille Odile — both grandmothers. Lena’s the godmother. Then they lost. The 8-Ball said very doubtful. She texts me the O Antiphons at dusk. Monday night she called at ten to one to argue about Pius, and won the point fair. I told her I’ve been sleeping in Danny’s bed. She said somebody ought to. When the Pope went down she texted within the minute: is he alright, are you. Christmas Eve she held the phone up to a bonfire on the levee so I could hear it burn. After Midnight Mass she wrote from the steps of Holy Rosary: an hour behind me, like she said. She’d mailed me *The Moviegoer* before the last night. Christmas night she told me how Réveillon went, and about the place her mother sets for her grandmother. Then she said her mama worked at Memorial. Nothing else. Holy Family: they lost to Tampa in overtime — ‘They’re resting.’ Fr. Dom took the short form; hers read the long one, and we’re not discussing it. Sunday night we whispered for two hours because Nonna was asleep in her chair, and she whispered too, from her back steps. I read her her own margins; she argued with the girl who wrote them. I told her Dad went in. ‘And Danny drank it.’ Julian calls at ten his time. Tuesday she called from behind the register at her father’s market — home field; her father’s making the musician a gumbo. I told her what Danny asked about the third. If Pop won’t get out of the truck, she says, I get in. She said she wouldn’t call as much. Then she said she’d call. Wednesday nothing. Thursday at dawn, the morning after Julian landed, she called from the river with beignets. She said she’d call. She asked if I asked Ma who the candle was for. No. You don’t. New Year’s Eve she texted at my midnight, an hour early for her. At hers it came the second the year turned — before the fireworks. I know what that means. Then the river on fire, and Julian beside it. New Year’s Day I called her from the garage at the half, and she said, You called *me*. Saturday night she called the house — Ma answered and talked to her for ten minutes. Two hours on the kitchen phone, her mother’s cordless dying twice. Her grandmother made the christening gown for Luc in 1985; it rode out the storm in Mémère’s cedar chest in Breaux Bridge. She had me be the priest so she could practice the promises. She thinks Binx doesn’t stop looking — he stops looking by himself. I told her Danny asked me something I can’t answer yet; she didn’t ask what. She asked how California was. ‘Come back, Youngstown.’ Two hours, and she never said Julian’s name. Lucille was baptized in the third quarter, and she didn’t get one word wrong. After that I called every night. Twelfth Night she got the baby in the king cake. Friday she said she hasn’t been fair to Julian, and she’s going to fix it. Sunday she landed: come find me tomorrow. Monday I couldn’t find her — not at 217, not at the twelve-ten. She came into Hale’s seminar a step behind him with a king cake, and the only chair left was next to mine. She was polite to me for fifteen minutes. Then Dido. Tuesday morning Julian put up a picture from their dinner Monday — birthday dinner, two days late. She’s tagged. She’d said call me after. I didn’t. At the mailboxes she asked about my break, and I told her as far as Denver, and Ma’s words about the coffee. ‘Tell her I’m glad.’ The baptism was lovely. Tuesday night at St. Brendan’s she had the whole thing organized by half past eight, in a whisper, and put me on the table with Becca. When the TV said trapped she left the room. Julian went. Wednesday at the table she met Skye. She said no pictures at the table, and I argued with her about it in front of everybody. That night at the desk: Skye’s envelope was the biggest. ‘Tell her thank you. From Newman.’

response: “I’ll tell her.”
“Good.” She hands the box across to Priya. “Goodnight, Jack.” She goes up the east stairs.
Priya puts the box in the safe and shuts it and spins the dial, and looks at him over the top of the desk. “Costigan. You look like a man who’s been to church.”
“She’ll want it in writing.”
“Then write it.” She hands the box across to Priya, and goes up the east stairs.
Priya puts the box in the safe and shuts it and spins the dial, and looks at him over the top of the desk. “Costigan. You look like a man who’s been to church.”
He nods.
She waits a second for more, and there isn’t any. She hands the box across to Priya and goes up the east stairs.
Priya puts the box in the safe and shuts it and spins the dial, and looks at him over the top of the desk. “Costigan. You look like a man who’s been to church.”

s14a.slug: WEDNESDAY · 10:42 PM · DELGADO HALL, THE FRONT STEPS
body: He goes back out the way he came in and sits down on the front steps. The quad is dark. Ferrer Tower is done chiming for the night, and the bike racks are full, and somebody’s sprinkler out by the lot is ticking around on the grass.

body.text: His bag is on the step beside him. In the front pocket, the tin: eleven, her count. In the side pocket, his own pack, one fewer than it rode home with. His thumb finds the lighter in his coat pocket and stays on the wheel.
body.else: His bag is on the step beside him. In the front pocket, the tin: eleven, her count. In the side pocket, his own pack, as it rode home. His thumb finds the lighter in his coat pocket and stays on the wheel.

response: He takes one out of his own pack and lights it with his shoulder to the quad. The smoke goes up past the dark windows of four and comes apart there. It doesn’t help. He smokes it to the filter anyway and puts it out on the step and puts the end in his pocket.
The front door is heavy, and he lets it be heavy. Inside, the radio on the desk is still on Haiti, and he goes in past it.
He puts the pack back in the side pocket and runs the zipper shut. Somebody laughs out in the lot, two people, and a car door, and the sprinkler comes around again.
The front door is heavy, and he lets it be heavy. Inside, the radio on the desk is still on Haiti, and he goes in past it.
He opens the tin on his knee, under the light from the lobby, and counts them with one finger.
Eleven.
He shuts it, and puts it back in the front pocket, and zips the pocket.
The front door is heavy, and he lets it be heavy. Inside, the radio on the desk is still on Haiti, and he goes in past it.

body: Theo is asleep. Jack can hear it across the room, long and even, the blazer a dark shape on its hanger on the closet door. The light off the quad comes in under the blind and goes up the wall. Down the hall a door, and Doug telling somebody on a headset to go left, and then the building settles.
The closet door that won’t latch unless you lift it has come open again by a crack, and the light finds the top shelf.

body.text: The can for the girl who called is up there, in the shape in the dust on Theo’s side, a little too small for it.
body.else: The can for the girl who called is up there on his own half, and across the divider, the clean place where the bag sat.
